lines.note: Nusumitori means stealing or taking by theft. This opening confirms the preceding page's Nuſu- catchword without turning that catchword into running text.

runs.text: Certa maneira de ſalſa, ou eſcaueche,

lines.note: Nuta is described as a sauce or pickling preparation. The dictionary's Portuguese comparison is retained rather than replaced by a modern recipe definition.
Explains preparing namasu with the sauce and begins the compound nutanamasu. Namaſu occurs within Portuguese prose, while the final Nu- starts a Japanese expression.
Completes nutanamasu, defined as namasu made with this preparation. The scan has Namaſu feito, not the OCR's fused Namaſuafeito; cõ retains its nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: Certa iguaria feita com este eſcaue-

lines.note: Nutaaye names food prepared with this dressing. The divided eſcaue-che is a Portuguese word, not a change of headword.
Nutaaye ni suru means preparing food in this manner. The final co- begins comer in the following continuation.
Completes o comer desta maneira, preparing the food this way. This closes the culinary entry.
Nutana or nutanamono describes a dirty or slovenly person. The alternative marker l and the printed cedilla in çuja are retained.
Completes the description as ill-kept, careless, or lazy. The historical priguiçoſa is not normalized to a modern spelling.
This independent headword refers the reader back to Nuta, where the compound has already been explained. Nuta is the upright cross-reference target after italic Vide.

runs.text: Dono, ſenhor, ou ſenhora de qualquer

lines.note: Nushi denotes the owner or master, male or female, of something. The scan supports ſenhora rather than OCR ſenbora.
Completes de qualquer couſa, extending ownership to any object. This ends the first of the separate nushi senses.

runs.text: Vos, ou tu, falando com gente baixa.

lines.note: Records nushi as second-person address, glossed vos or tu when speaking to people considered lower in status. This is the source's register description.
Here nushi is a lacquer craftsman, distinct from the preceding owner and pronoun senses. Vruxi names the material within the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Caſa onde ſe faz esta obra de Vruxi.

lines.note: Nushiya is the workshop where this lacquer work is done. Vruxi is again a Japanese material name embedded in Portuguese prose.
Nue is identified only as a bird with this name. The brief gloss does not itself describe the later familiar composite creature.

The decorated P belongs to Appato, giving PAppato, an adverb of sudden rising or spreading. OCR mistook the initial's ornament for a paragraph mark and lost the headword; its full six-line block is included in the owning crop.
Describes dust, waves, or flame rising. The scan reads ondas, not OCR onãas; laba- continues into labareda below.
Completes labareda, a tongue or blaze of flame. The decorative initial alongside this continuation is not additional text.
Gives pararito and fararito as alternative adverbs. The initial letter is P in the first form and f in the second; their contrast is visible and should not be flattened to two identical forms.

runs.text: Modo de ſoar algũa couſa que

lines.note: Introduces the sound made by something falling. The scan's ſoar corrects OCR ſoor; the subject continues on the next row.
Gives falling grains as the sound example and then introduces another sense. The verb is cae, not OCR cac, and this continuation is physically indented beside the initial.

runs.text: Totalmente, ou ſem ficar nada. Vt,

lines.note: Adds 'completely, without anything remaining'. Para- begins the Japanese example; its P is upright, not part of italic Vt.
Completes pararito tatta, all getting up or departing with none remaining. The Portuguese explanation continues below.
Completes the statement that no one remained. This belongs to pararito tatta, not the following destruction example.
Pararito uchikuzusu means destroying completely. The P belongs to the upright Japanese example, and ſẽ abbreviates the Portuguese sem.
Completes the total-destruction gloss: leaving nothing. It closes the extended pararito entry.
Patto describes something suddenly rising and spreading. The scan has two t types, agreeing with patto in the example below; OCR Pato lost one.

runs.text: lhar algũa couſa como fumo. Vt,

lines.note: Completes espalhar and gives smoke as an example. Chiqemu- starts chikemuri, the blood mist or vapor described in the quotation. Native enlargement in the second pass reveals the faint third stroke of m, correcting OCR n.
Completes chikemuri ga patto tatta, the blood vapor suddenly rising. Yax. is an upright citation label; va continues into vapor without a visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: por do ſangue ſe aleuantou, & eſpalhou.

lines.note: Completes vapor and translates the blood mist rising and spreading. This confirms the interpretation of the divided Japanese compound.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de acertar com a ſe-

lines.note: Paxxito describes striking or hitting decisively. The gloss begins with an arrow and continues to a lance below; the initial P is upright.
Completes seta and gives the example paxshito atatta, landing a hit. The Japanese P is not part of the italic example-introducer Vt.

runs.text: Deu, ou acertou bem no aluo, &c.

lines.note: Completes atatta and explains hitting the target squarely. The physical split is retained rather than joining the Japanese verb across rows.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de dar couçes a beſta.

lines.note: Pinpin describes an animal kicking. The enlarged two-line P and following capital I replace OCR Dinpin; the full initial is included in this row's crop.
Uma ga pinpin to hanuru describes a horse kicking or springing with its legs. The scan supports pinpinto fanuru, not the malformed hint based on pinpiuto faruru; caualo is also restored.
Completes the translation: the horse kicks. The printed unaccented da and plain c in couces are retained rather than harmonized with couçes above.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de estar muito juſta,

lines.note: Pixxito describes a very tight fit or close insertion. The headword begins with P, not OCR F; the running header above nevertheless visibly says O and is preserved as printed.
Completes the definition as something tightly pressed or inserted. Its actual continuation indentation is recorded.
Ponpon or poponto introduces an imitative sound. The initial P spans two rows and the following O is a printed capital; the corrupt D and mixed italic O in OCR are removed.

runs.text: ſoar o tabaquinho de Iapão, ou eſpingardas quã-

lines.note: Describes the sound of the object called tabaquinho de Iapão, or of guns. The source does not identify the object further here; tabaquinho is retained literally and quã- begins quando.
Completes quando and specifies the noise when the guns are discharged. The historical deſparão spelling is kept.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de ſubir a flamma,

lines.note: Poppoto describes a flame rising. The clear repeated p types and the Portuguese flamma recover the entry from OCR Foquoro and femmna.
Honoo ga poppoto tachinoboru illustrates a flame flaring upward. The repeated poppoto is visible; the line division occurs inside tachinoboru.

runs.text: Subir a flamma, ou labareda com

lines.note: Completes tachinoboru and starts the explanation of a flame or blaze rising forcefully. The scan reads flamma rather than OCR flanima.
Completes com furia, specifying vigorous flaring. This closes the P entries before the large Q section heading.

The decorated Q and following E form the headword QE; they are not an isolated numeral 1. Ke suru is glossed as transforming, with Transfi- continuing below. The complete crop shows the initial and ornament beside six text rows; the seventh continuation remains indented below the ornament.
Completes transfigurar-se and describes appearing in another form. The scan has for, not OCR ſor, and no terminal hyphen is added to this physical division.

runs.text: ma, ou figura, como o Demo-

lines.note: Completes forma, then compares the transformation to the devil appearing in human guise. The divided word is Demo-nio, not the OCR's Deino-nio.
Completes Demonio and the example of appearing in a human body. This is the dictionary's religious illustration of transformation.
Begins an example of a Buddha manifesting as a human. Fotoqe is the printed Japanese spelling here; xita- begins the honorific expression completed below.

Completes xitamǒ and translates the Buddha's appearance in human form. The decorative Q's lower strokes were misrecognized as extra characters; those artifacts are removed, while the actual mǒ and Portuguese text are retained.
Completes the translation as a human appearance. This last continuation remains indented below the decorative initial, which ends beside the preceding mǒ row.

runs.text: Cauſa, ou achaq̃ dalgũa couſa. Vt,

lines.note: Ke is defined as the cause or occasion of something. The final mark on achaq̃ abbreviates the ending of achaque; the example begins sono ke ni below rather than adding a modernized definition.

runs.text: Por ißo foy mal, ou mao. B.

lines.note: Completes sono ke ni warukatta, explained as being bad or going badly for that reason. The scan reads foy, not OCR for; B. is an upright low-register label.
Ke here means a ruled line; ke wo hiku means drawing such a line. The paired Riſca and Riſcar distinguish the noun from the action.

runs.text: Couſa ordinaria, ou de cote: não ſe vſa

lines.note: Ke denotes the ordinary or everyday, contrasted with festive or exceptional use. The Portuguese states that this sense is not used alone, continuing below.
Completes the warning that ke occurs in compounds and gives ke no kirumono, everyday clothing. The scan reads compoſição and qirumono, correcting both malformed OCR words.
Completes vestido and introduces kehare, the ordinary/festive contrast. The right-edge Tẽ begins tempo with a nasal abbreviation, not OCR rẽ.

runs.text: po ordinario ſem festa, & concurſo de gente,

lines.note: Describes ordinary time without a festival or gathering of people. This is the first half of the contrast explained by kehare.
Adds festive time and introduces ke no fuku, ordinary clothing. The example remains upright Japanese after the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Vestido ordinario: hoc vide infràſuo loco.

lines.note: Defines ordinary clothing and directs the reader to its own entry below. The mark in infrà is a grave, not the OCR tilde; the tight printed join with ſuo is retained.
Ke here means hair; ke ga tatsu means the hair standing on end. Arripia- continues as remſe below, with a small visible line-end division mark rather than a sentence stop.
Completes the hair-standing-on-end explanation, then introduces shedding feathers or hair. The printed Qeuo ſuru is retained even though the construction may seem unusual to a modern reader.

runs.text: rem as aues a pena, ou animaes os cabelos.

lines.note: Completes Mudarem and describes birds changing feathers or animals shedding hair. No extra verb form is supplied from modern expectation.
Ke also denotes fish scales in the usage described here. Ke wo toru is glossed as scaling a fish, continued below.

runs.text: camar o peixe. Palaura que ſe vſa em algũas

lines.note: Completes eſcamar and restricts this lexical use geographically. The restriction continues into Cami on the next row.
Limits the fish-scale word to some parts of Cami. The regional Japanese name occurs within the Portuguese explanation and is marked for optional whole-word font review.

runs.text: Dar com o pè para diante. Vt,

lines.note: Ke, keru, keta is the historical kicking verb, here striking forward with the foot. The following quotation illustrates the action.
Begins the example of kicking a pillow lying down with one's foot. The Japanese macura and emphatic fattatozo are preserved as printed.

Completes the kicking action and supplies the source label and book 2. Taif. is retained as the chosen reading of the worn upright label; its final f is less secure than the rest and is not silently expanded to a title.

runs.text: botou com o pè a almofada que estaua no chão

lines.note: Translates striking or propelling the pillow that was on the floor with the foot. The historical Portuguese estaua and chão remain unchanged.
Finishes the sudden kicking example, then introduces mari wo keru, playing ball with the foot. The scan reads pel, not OCR pol, and no terminal hyphen is supplied before la below.

runs.text: la com o pè como he custume em Iapão.

lines.note: Completes pella and specifies the Japanese custom of kicking the ball. Iapão is Portuguese, not an embedded Japanese word for the typeface-term list.
Keage means raising something by a kick. The scan ends with aleuantar and a comma, not OCR aleuantao.; its objects continue on the next page.
